R03-F-01: Modern moral intuition tends to reserve its highest praise for the gift that expects nothing in return. A present given with an eye to what will come back seems to us slightly tarnished, closer to a trade dressed up in ribbon than to generosity. Anthropologists who have studied exchange in a wide range of societies have long found this intuition puzzling, not because people elsewhere are more calculating, but because in most places the obligation to return is understood as part of what a gift is. To receive is to accept a tie; to fail to reciprocate is not merely rude but a refusal of the relationship the gift proposed. Consider how carefully the timing and size of a return are managed in many communities. A neighbour who sends back a dish of sweets on the very evening she received one has not discharged a debt so much as declined a friendship; the speed of her reply announces that she wants the account closed. A return that matches the original exactly carries a similar message. What sustains the bond is a return that comes later and differs slightly in value, so that one party is always, for the moment, a little in the other's debt. On this view the imbalance is not a flaw to be corrected but the mechanism by which the relationship is kept running: an account that is never quite settled is an account that remains open. Seen in this light, the free gift is less an ideal than an anomaly. A gift that truly demanded nothing would create no tie, and a society composed only of such gifts would be a collection of strangers who happened to hand each other things. It is telling that the gifts we most often describe as free, such as anonymous donations, are precisely those designed to prevent any relationship between giver and receiver from forming. None of this means that the obligation to return is always benign. Where one party can give far more than the other could ever repay, the gift becomes an instrument of domination: the receiver is bound by a debt that cannot be cleared, and gratitude hardens into dependence. Patrons have long understood this, and so have recipients of charity, who sometimes refuse help precisely because they cannot answer it. The lesson, however, is not that we should aspire to gifts without strings. It is that the strings must be ones the receiver is able to hold. A generous act, properly understood, is calibrated to the other person's capacity to reply.
R03-F-02: The story is told in so many introductory textbooks that it has come to seem like common sense. Once upon a time, it runs, people traded goods directly: a farmer with grain who wanted shoes had to find a shoemaker who happened to want grain. Because such a coincidence was rare, someone eventually hit on the idea of a commodity everyone would accept, such as shells, salt or metal, and money was born. Credit and debt, in this account, come last, a refinement that becomes possible only once coins are available to measure what is owed. The difficulty is that the story describes a world no one has found. Anthropologists who went looking for economies in which neighbours regularly exchanged goods by barter have, on the whole, come back empty-handed. What they found instead, in village after village, was something closer to running accounts. A woman who needs a pot from her neighbour simply takes it, and both understand that something will be owed; the debt may be repaid in grain at harvest, in labour at a wedding, or never precisely at all. Among people who expect to keep living beside one another, the problem of the double coincidence of wants scarcely arises, because no one needs the exchange to be completed on the spot. Barter does occur, but in revealing places. It appears between strangers who do not expect to meet again, between groups who distrust each other, and among people who were once used to money and have been cut off from it, such as prisoners trading cigarettes or townspeople whose currency has collapsed. In each case barter is a response to the absence of trust, not the primitive condition out of which trust and credit later grew. Defenders of the textbook story sometimes reply that it was never intended as history. It is, they say, a thought experiment showing why a medium of exchange is useful, and its value does not depend on whether any society actually passed through a barter stage. This is a fair point as far as it goes. But the thought experiment is not idle. By placing money first and debt last, it teaches us to see money as a neutral token that merely smooths trade between independent individuals, rather than as a way of recording obligations between people already bound to one another. If the record points the other way, the more natural conclusion is that money began as a method of keeping score.
R03-F-03: We tend to picture hospitality as the purest form of generosity: a door opened to someone who has no claim on us and nothing to give in return. The picture is not false, but it omits half of what the practice involves. In the many traditions in which welcoming strangers is held to be a sacred duty, the welcome is also a careful exercise of authority. The host decides where the guest will sit, what he will eat, when he will speak and, eventually, when he will leave. To accept hospitality is to accept, for a time, a place inside someone else's order. This asymmetry is not incidental. A stranger arriving at a settlement is, from the settlement's point of view, an unknown quantity: he may be a trader, a refugee, a spy or a raider. Hospitality converts this uncertain figure into a guest, someone whose position is defined and whose conduct is now governed by rules that the host administers. The rituals that so often accompany a welcome, such as the offering of water, the sharing of salt or bread and the formal exchange of names, can be read as stages in this conversion. The guest who eats at the host's table has implicitly agreed not to harm the household, and the host, in turn, has made himself responsible for the guest's safety against third parties. It is significant, too, that hospitality is so often limited in time. Many customs specify that a guest may stay a few days before his status must change; after that he becomes a dependant who works, a kinsman by adoption, or simply an unwelcome burden. The welcome is generous precisely because it is temporary. A guest who could stay forever on a guest's terms would gradually unsettle the household's order, and the host would cease to be master of his own house. Some philosophers have pressed for an ideal of unconditional hospitality, a welcome that asks no questions and sets no limits. As a corrective to the suspicion with which outsiders are often treated, the ideal has force. But taken literally it would dissolve the very relation it seeks to purify. Hospitality requires a host, someone who is at home and who can therefore offer a place; if every condition is removed, there is no longer anyone in a position to welcome. The authority that makes us uneasy is not a corruption of hospitality. It is the condition that allows a stranger to be received at all.
R03-F-04: A parable that became famous in the second half of the twentieth century asks us to imagine a pasture open to all. Each herder, reasoning that the benefit of an extra animal is his alone while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, adds another, and then another, until the grass is gone and all are ruined. The moral usually drawn is stark: resources held in common will be destroyed unless they are divided into private plots or placed under the control of the state. The parable is persuasive, but it describes something that most actual commons are not. In many villages, pastures, woodlots, fishing ponds and irrigation channels have been shared for generations without being exhausted, and not because the villagers were unusually selfless. They were governed by rules. A household might be allowed to graze only as many animals as it could feed through the winter from its own fields; grazing might move between sections of the hill in a fixed rotation; a watchman, paid in grain, might patrol the boundary, and offenders might face fines that rose with each repeated offence. The herders of the parable have no such rules, no means of watching one another and no way of punishing those who cheat. What the parable describes is not a commons but open access, a resource that belongs to no community at all. This does not mean that village commons always survive. They tend to fail in recognisable circumstances: when outsiders who are not bound by local rules can enter freely, when a distant authority overrides local arrangements with regulations that villagers neither understand nor respect, when migration thins the community so much that no one is left to keep watch, or when a sudden rise in the value of the resource makes cheating more tempting than it has ever been. These are real dangers. But they are dangers to particular institutions, not proof that shared ownership is doomed by human nature. The practical lesson is that the familiar choice between private property and state control is too narrow. To say so is not to romanticise village life; such arrangements can be strict, and some are unequal, giving larger shares to households that hold more land. Even so, a third possibility, communities managing their own resources by rules they have made and can enforce, has a long record of success, and policy that ignores it may destroy working arrangements in the name of preventing a tragedy that was never going to happen.
R03-F-05: For a long time the dominant attitude of academic history towards oral tradition was one of polite suspicion. A story passed from mouth to mouth over many generations, it was argued, must accumulate errors as surely as a manuscript copied by careless scribes, and in the absence of any original against which to check it, the historian had no way of telling the accurate parts from the embellishments. Against this, a more recent and more sympathetic current has insisted that societies without writing developed techniques of memorisation of extraordinary precision, and that their traditions deserve to be treated as archives in their own right. Each side, I want to suggest, misconceives the object it is arguing about. The error both share is to assume that an oral tradition is trying to do what a written chronicle does, namely preserve a record of past events for its own sake, and to differ only on how well it succeeds. Traditions are rarely maintained for that purpose. A genealogy recited at the installation of a chief exists to establish that he is entitled to the office; an account of the first settlers exists to explain why one lineage holds the best land and another serves as its ritual guardians. Because the tradition answers to present needs, it changes when those needs change, and its changes are not random. Lines that no longer matter drop out; ancestors who connect currently allied groups acquire importance; the long, uneventful middle of the past is compressed, so that the founders seem only a few generations removed from those who remember their grandparents. This is precisely why the sceptic's analogy with the copied manuscript is misleading. Random copying errors cannot be corrected without an original, but distortions that follow from a known function can, at least in part, be anticipated and read through. A historian who understands that a genealogy is a charter for office will be cautious about its middle generations and its convenient links, while attending closely to details that serve no present interest and are therefore unlikely to have been invented. Nor is all content equally fluid: formulaic songs, names of places and fixed ritual phrases are often transmitted with a fidelity that ordinary narrative never achieves, even when no one any longer understands what they mean. None of this licenses the opposite romanticism. A tradition that is reliable about the shape of an ancient migration may be quite wrong about who led it, and no technique of memorisation can protect a story from a community's interest in retelling it. Written sources, it should be added, are hardly exempt from the same pressures; charters and chronicles were also composed to justify claims, and historians learned long ago to read them against the grain. Oral tradition, approached in that spirit, is neither an archive nor a fiction. It is a record of what a community needed its past to be, and that is itself a kind of evidence about the past.
R03-F-06: It has become common for conservation projects and agricultural agencies to announce that they have 'validated' some piece of local knowledge. Fishers' accounts of where a species gathers to spawn are checked against tagging data; herders' claims about which plants their animals avoid in a dry year are tested in feeding trials; farmers' weather signs are compared with rainfall records. When the local claim survives, it is welcomed into the scientific literature, and the project is praised for taking seriously people whose expertise was long ignored. This is an improvement on simple dismissal. Yet the language of validation carries assumptions that deserve more scrutiny than they usually receive. The first is that local knowledge is a set of separate statements, each of which can be lifted out and checked on its own. Much of what farmers and fishers know does not take this form. A farmer who decides when to sow may attend at once to the flowering of a particular tree, the behaviour of ants, the smell of the soil and the memory of the last three seasons, weighing them against one another in ways she could not easily put into words. Test any one of these signs in isolation and it may predict rainfall poorly; to conclude that the farmer's knowledge has failed would be to mistake a judgement for a list of rules. What is being evaluated is not what she knows but a fragment translated into a form the evaluator can handle. The second assumption is that the direction of authority runs one way. Science sets the standard, local knowledge applies for admission, and once admitted it belongs to the literature rather than to the people who held it. Communities have sometimes found that knowledge about medicinal plants or fishing grounds, once published, was used by outsiders in ways they had no say in. Validation, in other words, can be a means of transfer as much as of recognition. It would be wrong to conclude that local knowledge should be shielded from testing altogether. Some local beliefs are mistaken, as some scientific ones are, and the communities that hold them revise them in the light of experience more often than romantic accounts allow. The objection is not to checking but to a procedure in which only one side checks. Where farmers help decide which questions are asked and how the results will be used, and where scientific claims are also tested against their observations, the two bodies of knowledge can correct each other. That is a more demanding arrangement than validation, and a more honest one.
R03-F-07: One of the first lessons of economics is that money is fungible. A rupee earned is the same as a rupee found, a rupee received as a gift or a rupee won at cards; since each can buy exactly what the others can, a rational person should be indifferent to where a sum came from and should spend it according to a single ranking of needs. This is what makes money so useful. It strips goods of their particular histories and renders them comparable, and it lets a stranger in one town trade with a stranger in another without either needing to know anything about the other's life. Ordinary households, however, behave as though they had never heard the lesson. Coins for the temple are kept in a separate tin; a grandmother's gift to a newborn goes into a savings account that no one will touch for rent even in a hard month; the money a woman earns from tailoring is spent on her children's schooling, while her husband's wages go to food and the loan; a windfall is spent on a celebration that the same sum, arriving as salary, would never have funded. Money that arrives in one way is marked, set aside and spent in another, as though each sum carried a label that its owners were bound to respect. Nor are such habits confined to poor households; in one form or another they appear in families at every level of income. The standard response is to call this mental accounting and to treat it as a lapse, a cognitive shortcut that serves people tolerably on the whole but leads them into avoidable errors. The errors are real. A family that keeps savings in a low-interest account reserved for a daughter's wedding while borrowing at a ruinous rate to repair the roof is paying heavily for a distinction that, in purely financial terms, does not exist. Yet to describe earmarking only as a mistake is to miss what it accomplishes. The grandmother's gift is set apart because it is a relationship as much as a sum: spending it on rent would feel like dissolving the bond it expressed. The tailor's earnings are spent on schooling because keeping them distinct allows her to claim, within the household, a sphere of decision that pooled money would not give her. Labels on money are the means by which people make it say something about who they are to one another. It may be objected that this shows only that people attach feelings to money, not that money itself ceases to be fungible. In the market, after all, the tailor's rupee buys exactly what her husband's does, and no shopkeeper asks about its origin. The objection is correct about the shopkeeper. But it concedes the point that matters. Fungibility holds where people have agreed to ignore the histories of sums, as in impersonal trade, and fails where they have not, as in the household, the family ceremony and the circle of friends who lend to one another. The single, featureless money of the textbook, then, is not a natural property of currency that social life afterwards distorts. It is an arrangement that holds in certain settings and that people are constantly unmaking elsewhere. To see this is not to deny that the arrangement is valuable, or that families sometimes pay dearly for their labels; it is to recognise that the indifference to origins which economics takes as its starting point is itself a social achievement, and a local one.
R03-F-08: In many parts of the world, groups of neighbours, co-workers or traders meet at regular intervals and each contributes a fixed sum to a common pot, which is then handed in its entirety to one member. At the next meeting the process is repeated and the pot goes to someone else, until every member has received it once and the cycle ends or begins again. The order may be fixed by lot, by agreement or, in some versions, by bidding, with the member who most urgently wants the money accepting a smaller pot and the difference shared among the rest. Such rotating associations go by dozens of local names, and for a long time development economists regarded them as makeshift substitutes for banks, ingenious but destined to disappear once formal credit reached the people who used them. That prediction has fared poorly. The associations persist among people who have bank accounts, and they have travelled with migrants into cities where banks are on every corner. Their persistence is puzzling on a narrow financial view. For those who receive the pot early, the arrangement is an interest-free loan; for those who receive it late, it is a savings scheme that pays no interest at all, and that exposes them to the risk that an early recipient will stop contributing once he has been paid. A late member could, it seems, do better by saving the same sums in a bank, and an early member would be the obvious candidate for default. The usual solutions to the puzzle point to discipline. Saving alone requires a resolve that many people find hard to sustain; a contribution owed to a group that meets every month, whose members will notice and remember a missed payment, supplies that resolve from outside. This is surely part of the answer. But it treats the problem as one between the saver and her own weaker self, whereas members themselves often describe it differently. What makes saving hard, they say, is not temptation so much as other people: the brother who needs money for a wedding, the cousin whose shop has failed, the neighbour whose child is ill. A sum in a bank account is visible to such claims and difficult to refuse. A sum owed to the association is not available, and saying so is an excuse that kin and neighbours recognise as legitimate. On this reading the association is not a crude version of a bank but an instrument for managing obligations, one that uses a debt to the group to shelter money from other debts that are harder to decline. The reading also explains why the associations depend so heavily on the density of the ties among their members. The same social pressure that makes a refusal to a cousin acceptable is what keeps the early recipient paying; where members can move away without consequence, or barely know one another, the associations break down, and stories of a member who vanished with the pot are common enough to show that the risk is not imaginary. None of this implies that formal finance has nothing to offer the people who join such groups, or that the associations are always wise; members of bidding versions sometimes accept heavy discounts out of desperation, and the losses from a collapse can be severe. The point is narrower and, I think, more instructive. The rotating association survives not because its members lack access to something better but because it does something that an ordinary bank account, by design, does not: it makes a sum of money socially unavailable. The question its persistence raises is less why the poor lack banks than what banks, as they are usually designed, lack.
